blocks.content: Picture a very fast server, sitting in a data centre with enormous bandwidth to spare, sending data to a phone on a slow, patchy connection. The server can produce data far faster than the phone's connection can carry it away, and far faster than the phone's app can process it once it arrives.

If the server just kept blasting data as fast as it possibly could, with no regard for whether the other side could actually keep up, the phone's incoming buffer would fill up completely. Any more data that arrived would simply have nowhere to go and would be dropped, which means bandwidth and effort were spent sending something that now has to be sent all over again.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784013199627-777112125.png
blocks.alt: A fast sender blasts data faster than the receiver's buffer can absorb it, and the overflow is dropped

blocks.content: 1. The Problem: A Fast Sender And A Struggling Receiver
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: A Fast Sender And A Struggling Receiver

blocks.content: There are actually two separate ways a receiver can fall behind. Its network connection itself might be slow and weak, so data piles up before it even reaches the application. Or the connection might be perfectly fine but the receiving application is simply busy, doing other work and not reading the incoming data out of its buffer quickly enough.

Either way, the receiver ends up with a buffer, a fixed chunk of memory set aside to hold incoming data before the application reads it, that is filling up faster than it is draining. Once that buffer is completely full, the operating system has no choice but to drop any further incoming data. The sender eventually notices the loss and has to resend the very same data, burning bandwidth and time twice over for work that should have only happened once.

blocks.title: Wasted Work
blocks.content: A dropped segment is not free. It still cost the sender CPU time to build and transmit, it still used up bandwidth on the way, and now the exact same bytes have to be prepared and sent all over again. Slowing down proactively is almost always cheaper than losing data and retransmitting it.
2. Flow Control Defined, And Why It Is Not Congestion Control
blocks.text: 2. Flow Control Defined, And Why It Is Not Congestion Control

blocks.content: Flow control is the mechanism that solves exactly this problem, and its job is narrow and specific: make sure a sender never sends data faster than the receiving side can actually process and store it. That is the entire job, nothing more.

Notice what this definition does not mention at all: the network in between. Flow control is a conversation between exactly the two endpoints of one single connection, the sender and the receiver, about how much the receiver can currently handle. It has nothing to do with routers, congested links, or how many other connections happen to be sharing the path along the way. That separate problem, protecting the shared network itself from being overwhelmed, is congestion control, and it is the very next topic in this module.

In flow control, the receiver is always the one in the driver's seat. It is the receiver's available buffer space, not the sender's willingness or the network's capacity, that decides how much data can be in flight at any moment. Keep that ownership straight and the rest of this topic falls into place easily.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784013201753-23424913.png
blocks.alt: Flow control is a local conversation between one sender and one receiver, congestion control involves the shared network carrying many connections

blocks.title: One Line Version
blocks.content: Flow control protects the receiver. Congestion control protects the network. Same symptom, a sender slowing down, but two completely different reasons and two completely different scopes.
3. The Receive Window: How The Receiver Sets The Pace
blocks.text: 3. The Receive Window: How The Receiver Sets The Pace

blocks.content: The mechanism the receiver uses to communicate its capacity is called the receive window. As part of every acknowledgment it sends back, tying directly into the acknowledgment mechanism you already know from how TCP achieves reliability, the receiver also includes a number: exactly how much more data it is currently willing and able to accept.

The sender is required to respect this number. It must never have more unacknowledged data in flight toward that receiver than the receive window currently allows. If the window says 500 bytes, the sender can have at most 500 bytes of data out there waiting to be acknowledged, no matter how much more it is ready and eager to send.

This turns every single acknowledgment into two pieces of information at once: confirmation of what arrived safely, and a live instruction for how much more can be sent right now. The receive window is not set once and forgotten, it rides along on every acknowledgment and can change from one moment to the next.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784013203704-270025912.png
blocks.alt: The receiver advertises its receive window as part of every acknowledgment it sends back to the sender

4. A Worked Example With Real Numbers
blocks.text: 4. A Worked Example With Real Numbers

blocks.content: Concrete numbers make this click faster than any definition. Say a receiver advertises a window of 1000 bytes. The sender is now free to send up to 1000 bytes of data without waiting for anything back, but the moment it hits that limit, it must stop and wait for an acknowledgment before sending a single byte more.

Now suppose the receiving application is slow to read that data out of its buffer, perhaps it is busy processing the previous batch. The buffer is still holding most of that 1000 bytes when the acknowledgment goes out, so the receiver has much less room than before. Its next acknowledgment will advertise a smaller window, say 200 bytes instead of 1000, actively telling the sender to slow down and send less before checking in again.

The sender does not need to guess or estimate anything here. It simply reads the number the receiver gave it and obeys. This is what makes flow control so reliable: it is not a heuristic or a best effort estimate, it is an explicit, numeric instruction repeated on every acknowledgment.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784013205412-625211344.png
blocks.alt: Step by step, the sender sends up to the advertised window, waits for acknowledgment, then sends again within the new window

5. The Window Rises And Falls With The Buffer
blocks.text: 5. The Window Rises And Falls With The Buffer

blocks.content: The receive window is not a fixed ceiling, it is a live, constantly updated readout of exactly how much spare room the receiver has right now. Every single acknowledgment carries the current value, so the window is really a running commentary on the state of the receiver's buffer.

When the receiving application falls behind, the buffer fills and the window shrinks, sometimes step by step, sometimes suddenly if the application stalls completely. When that same application catches up and reads the buffered data out, room frees up and the very next acknowledgment reflects that by advertising a larger window again.

This constant rising and falling is exactly what lets one connection adapt smoothly to a receiver whose processing speed changes minute to minute: a phone app that is sometimes idle and sometimes busy, a background service that occasionally pauses for garbage collection. All of it gets handled automatically without either side needing to do anything special.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784013207139-759070296.png
blocks.alt: The receive window shrinks as the buffer fills and grows again as the application drains it

blocks.content: 6. The Doorway Analogy

Imagine trying to hand someone a huge stack of papers, one at a time, as fast as you possibly can. If they are still sorting through the papers you already handed them, continuing to shove more into their hands just makes everything fall on the floor. That mess, the dropped papers, is exactly what a receiver's dropped packets look like.

Flow control is the receiver saying, clearly and explicitly, I can take three more right now, wait for me to catch up before handing me anything else. That short sentence is functionally identical to a receive window: a precise, current statement of capacity that the other side is expected to respect before offering more.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784013208920-880477847.png
blocks.alt: Handing over papers only as fast as the other person can sort through them, the same idea as a receive window

blocks.content: 7. The Zero Window: When The Receiver Says Stop Completely
blocks.text: 7. The Zero Window: When The Receiver Says Stop Completely

blocks.content: Sometimes a receiver's buffer becomes completely full, the application has stopped reading entirely, perhaps it crashed, perhaps it is stuck on something else. In that case the receiver can actually advertise a window size of zero. That is a completely valid, well understood signal, and it means exactly what it says: stop sending, I have no room at all right now.

A sender that receives a zero window does not give up or close the connection, it simply stops sending new data and waits. Periodically, it sends a small probe, essentially a check in message, to ask whether the receiver has freed up any space yet. Once the receiver's buffer has room again, its response to that probe will carry a nonzero window, and the sender resumes sending normally.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784013210520-130278708.png
blocks.alt: A completely full receiver advertises a zero window, the sender stops and periodically probes until room frees up

blocks.title: Why The Probe Exists
blocks.content: Without that periodic probe, there would be a real risk of a silent deadlock: the receiver frees up space and would happily accept more data, but has no data of its own to send back announcing that fact, and the sender is sitting there waiting indefinitely. The probe breaks that deadlock by having the sender proactively ask instead of waiting forever.
8. Flow Control vs Congestion Control, Side By Side
blocks.text: 8. Flow Control vs Congestion Control, Side By Side

blocks.content: These two mechanisms get confused constantly, and it is easy to see why: both of them result in a sender slowing down, and both of them work by shrinking how much data the sender is allowed to have in flight. But the reason behind the slowdown, and who is doing the asking, are completely different.

Flow control is entirely local. It is a private conversation between exactly one sender and one receiver about that receiver's own buffer space, and it has no idea that any other connection even exists. Congestion control is the opposite: it is about the shared links and routers in between, which are carrying traffic from potentially many different connections all at once, and it protects that shared infrastructure regardless of how healthy any individual receiver's buffer happens to be.

blocks.title: Same Symptom, Different Cause
blocks.content: If you remember nothing else from this comparison, remember this: a sender slowing down does not automatically mean the network is congested. It might just mean one receiver, on one connection, has a full buffer right now. Knowing which one is happening changes how you would debug a slow connection.
9. Why This Matters, And Common Mistakes
blocks.text: 9. Why This Matters, And Common Mistakes

blocks.content: This is not a theoretical concern. A fast API server sitting in a data centre, talking to a slow mobile client on a weak cellular connection, genuinely needs flow control every single day. Without it, the server could easily produce data far faster than the phone can absorb it, wasting bandwidth and battery on data that just gets dropped and has to be resent anyway.

The same story plays out anywhere a fast producer talks to a slower consumer: a backend service streaming data to a browser tab that is busy rendering, a file transfer to a device with a nearly full disk, a video call where one side's device is under heavy load. In every one of these cases, flow control is quietly doing its job in the background, and you likely never notice it working correctly. You only notice when it is missing.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784013213880-988315658.png
blocks.alt: Without flow control a fast API server overwhelms a slow phone connection, with flow control the same server paces itself to match
